analysis.one_liner: Taxes big investment funds $50,000 per excess single-family rental and funds down payment aid with the revenue.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the House with 4 sponsors and referred to two committees; no committee action or vote has taken place, and none is scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tax investment funds that pool outside money and own single-family rentals. It puts a 50% tax on any new single-family home such a fund buys, then charges $50,000 a year for every home the fund keeps beyond a shrinking limit — starting at 90% of its current holdings and stepping down over nine years to zero for hedge funds. It also takes away the mortgage interest and depreciation deductions for homes these funds own, bars Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Ginnie Mae from financing their mortgages, and sends the money raised into a trust fund for down payment assistance for families earning up to 120% of area median income. Organizations mainly building or rehabilitating homes are exempt, and so are homes used as an owner's own residence.
analysis.who_benefits: First-time and moderate-income homebuyers, who would face less competition from large investment funds bidding on single-family homes and could get down payment help from the new trust fund. Renters in markets where large funds own a big share of houses could benefit indirectly if funds sell off homes. Homebuilders and rehabbers are explicitly exempt from the tax, so they could buy and sell homes without penalty.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 50% excise tax on the fair market value of any new single-family residence acquired by a fund that pools money from investors, discouraging further large-scale purchases of houses.

Charges $50,000 per year for each home a fund keeps beyond a limit that shrinks over nine years — from 90% of its existing holdings down to zero for hedge funds — forcing a steady sell-off of existing single-family rentals.

Eliminates the mortgage interest and depreciation deductions on homes owned by covered funds, and bars Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Ginnie Mae from newly buying, lending on, or guaranteeing mortgages for these investors, cutting off federal mortgage backing.

Routes the tax revenue into a Housing Downpayment Trust Fund that makes grants to state housing finance agencies for down payment assistance, closing costs, and rate buydowns for families at or below 120% of area median income, with priority given to buyers of homes sold by covered funds.

analysis.who_pays: Large investment funds — hedge funds, private equity funds, and other pooled-money managers with $50 million or more in assets — that own single-family rentals, which face the new taxes, lost deductions, and lost access to government-backed mortgage finance. Their investors bear those costs. Indirectly, renters could face fewer rental options in the short term as funds are pushed to sell, and any buyer purchasing a home from a covered fund must sign a certification and could owe a $50,000 penalty for a false or missing report.

drawbacks.text: A forced sell-off could shrink the rental supply before owner-occupants absorb the homes, potentially raising rents for renters in the near term, especially where large funds own a big share of houses.

The tax applies to any pooled-money fiduciary with $50 million or more in net value or assets under management, a broad definition that could reach beyond classic hedge funds to other investment managers, and funds could restructure to fit the exemption that allows non-hedge-fund taxpayers to keep 50 homes.

Buyers of homes from covered funds must certify the sale is not a 'disqualified sale' and face a $50,000 penalty for a false or missing certification, adding a compliance burden to ordinary transactions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real affordability problem — large investment funds competing with families for single-family homes — and pairs the tax with a dedicated funding stream for down payment help. Its nine-year phase-down limits disruption to the rental market, but a 50% tax on new purchases and forced disposals could still tighten rental supply in the short run, and the broad definition of a covered taxpayer plus the carve-out allowing non-hedge-fund taxpayers to keep 50 homes creates avoidance and fairness questions. On balance it is designed as a strong push, not a fine-tuned one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the House on July 13, 2026, and sent to the Ways and Means and Financial Services committees, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Smith of Washington introduced the bill on July 13, 2026, joined by Reps. Ro Khanna, Nikema Williams of Georgia, and Linda Sanchez as cosponsors — 4 House members in all, all Democrats.
The House referred the bill to the Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the Financial Services Committee for the parts within their jurisdiction; neither committee has taken further action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large investment funds that own single-family rentals, which face no new taxes, lost deductions, or restrictions on selling to them because the bill has not moved. Nothing has changed for homebuyers yet either.

for.name: Adam Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its lead sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats sponsored the bill, but no vote has occurred and no opposition has been recorded in the congressional record yet.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and other pooled-money managers owning single-family rentals
industries.note: These funds face a 50% tax on new house purchases, a $50,000-per-home annual tax on a shrinking portfolio, lost deductions, and exclusion from Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Ginnie Mae mortgage backing. The bill is aimed squarely at forcing them out of single-family home ownership.
Organizations primarily engaged in constructing or rehabilitating single-family residences are exempt from the tax, so they could expand operations as funds sell off homes without penalty.

industries.industry: Government-backed mortgage finance (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, Ginnie Mae)
industries.note: The bill bars these agencies from newly purchasing, lending on, or guaranteeing mortgages made by covered large investors, reducing their single-family business with those investors while steering the housing finance system toward owner-occupants.

industries.industry: State housing finance agencies and mortgage lenders serving first-time buyers
industries.note: Down payment trust fund grants flow to state housing finance agencies to expand down payment assistance, closing cost help, and rate buydowns for moderate-income buyers.

analysis.trajectory: With only four House sponsors, dual committee referrals, and no hearing or markup scheduled, the bill follows the pattern of most tax bills: without support from the Ways and Means chairman or majority leadership, it is very unlikely to reach a floor vote before this Congress ends in January 2027.
